newsitem.title: GERMANY: Canada budget focus is jobs, not tax cuts - Martin.
newsitem.headline: Canada budget focus is jobs, not tax cuts - Martin.

text.p: Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin said on Saturday his budget for 1997-98, due for release on February 18, would focus on jobs creation and would not include broad new tax cuts.

After a meeting of finance ministers and central bankers from the Group of Seven industrialised nations, Martin and Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen told Reuters Canada's economic fundamentals were so healthy the country was feeling less pressure to follow U.S. policy moves.
They also said Canada's progress on fiscal consolidation was recognised at the G7 meeting by other members and by International Monetary Fund managing director Michel Camdessus.

"Our basic focus (in the budget) is jobs," Martin said. "Broad-based tax cuts would have to be paid for either through large increases in borrowing, which would result in higher interest rates and less jobs, or by large cuts in social programmes."
In the past, Canada has made selective tax cuts as incentives to vulnerable areas of the economy. "We haven't ruled those out, but broad-based tax cuts, no," Martin said.
Recent declines in Canadian interest rates have sharply boosted consumers' purchasing power and the economy as a whole, he said.

Canada projects its 1997 budget deficit will fall to 1.3 percent of gross domestic product, far below the 2.9-percent average for the G7 nations. Canada is not going to balance its budget overnight, "but we're going to get there someday," he said.

Thiessen, asked if Canada would feel pressure to raise interest rates if the U.S. Federal Reserve tightens as widely expected, said "whenever American rates go up, that always impacts Canada. But in our current situation, the underlying fundamentals are so good that we have a lot more room to manoeuvre."
He added, "Our inflation rate is lower than that in our major trading partner (the U.S.), and our economy has a wider measure of unused capacity, but we think that is going to narrow."
Martin said the G7 had agreed the major misalignments in exchange markets observed two years ago had been corrected, a reference to the dollar's recent rebound.
The G7 affirmed that exchange rates should reflect fundamentals and that excess volatility is undesirable.
"Our view is that currencies should reflect fundamentals, and as long as that is the case, things are unfolding as they should," Martin said.

One issue discussed by the G7 on which Canada has been particularly active, Martin said, is tax competition, in which nations engage in a "beggar-thy-neighbour" game of trying to attract industry by offering favourable tax treatment.
"The risk (is) that tax competition does not simply lead to a shifting, but it leads to a shrinking tax base," Martin said.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel has said he will be launching a new initiative on tax harmonisation on the European level in coming weeks, in an effort to stamp out tax havens. Germany, which has a reputation as a high-tax country, recently announced major corporate tax cuts due to take effect in 1999.
Martin said there was considerable optimism among G7 finance ministers about the overall global economy, particularly as Japan appears to be turning upward from its long downturn.
